paper_title: How the eye measures reality and virtual reality
abstract: If virtual reality systems are to make good on their name, designers must know how people perceive space in natural environments, in photographs, and in cinema. Perceivers understand the layout of a cluttered natural environment through the use of nine or more sources of information, each based on different assumptions—occlusion, height in the visual field, relative size, relative density, aerial per- spective, binocular disparities, accommodation, convergence, and motion perspective. The relative utility of these sources at different distances is compared, using their ordinal depth-threshold func- tions. From these, three classes of space around a moving observer are postulated: personal space, ac- tion space, and vista space. Within each, a smaller number of sources act in consort, with different rel- ative strengths. Given the general ordinality of the sources, these spaces are likely to be affine in character, stretching and collapsing with viewing conditions. One of these conditions is controlled by lens length in photography and cinematography or by field-of-view commands in computer graphics. These have striking effects on many of these sources of information and, consequently, on how the lay- out of a scene is perceived.
methodology: This paper presents a theoretical framework and synthesizes existing psychophysical data and logical considerations from a wide range of literature. It uses graphical coordinates to plot just noticeable differences (JNDs) in depth for various information sources as a function of distance, analogous to contrast sensitivity functions. The approach adopts an ordinal measurement scale to converge on a near-metric (probably affine) representation of space.
sample: Not applicable, as this is a theoretical review paper synthesizing findings from numerous studies involving human observers.
manipulated_features: Nine sources of information for depth perception: occlusion, height in the visual field, relative size, relative density, aerial perspective, binocular disparities, accommodation, convergence, and motion perspective.
Distance from the observer (0.5 m to 10,000 m).
Lens length in photography and cinematography (e.g., standard 50mm, long 500mm, short 25mm).
outcomes: Perception of layout (depth) in natural environments, photographs, and cinema.
Just noticeable difference (JND) in depth for two objects at different distances.
Relative efficacy of different depth cues.
Character of perceived space (Euclidean vs. affine).
key_findings: Perceivers use nine or more sources of information (occlusion, height in visual field, relative size, relative density, aerial perspective, binocular disparities, accommodation, convergence, and motion perspective) to understand cluttered environments.
The relative utility of these sources varies with distance, as shown by their ordinal depth-threshold functions.
Three classes of space around a moving observer are postulated: personal space (0-1.5 m), action space (1.5-30 m), and vista space (>30 m).
Within each space, a smaller number of sources act in consort with different relative strengths.
Personal space appears nearly Euclidean, while action and vista spaces are largely affine, stretching and collapsing with viewing conditions.

Lens length in photography/cinematography or field-of-view commands in computer graphics have striking effects on depth perception; a 500mm lens compresses depth by a factor of 10 (one log unit), while a 25mm lens expands depth by a factor of two (one-third log unit).
Occlusion provides depth thresholds of 0.1% or better, effective at all distances.
Relative size provides depth thresholds of about 3%, effective throughout the visible range.
Binocular disparities and motion perspective decline in utility to 10% at roughly 30 m, delimiting action space.
Accommodation and convergence are effective at close range, less than 3 m.
Adding information generally increases perceived depth and consistency/accuracy of depth judgments.
Individual differences in reliance on information sources are expected due to the multiplicity of cues and personal histories.
theories_referenced: Non-Euclidean nature of perceived space (Luneburg, 1947; Indow, 1990)
mechanisms: Occlusion: One object hiding another indicates the occluding object is in front.
Height in the visual field: Relations among object bases projected to the eye, assuming a ground plane and gravity.
Relative size: Angular extent of similar objects or textures on the retina.
Relative density: Projected number of similar objects or textures per solid visual angle.
Aerial perspective: Increasing indistinctness of objects with distance due to atmospheric moisture/pollutants.
Binocular disparity: Difference in relative position of an object projected on the retinas of the two eyes, yielding stereopsis or diplopia.
Accommodation: Change in eye lens shape to focus on objects at different distances.
Convergence: Angle between foveal axes of the two eyes, indicating distance.
Motion perspective: Field of relative motions of objects rigidly attached to a ground plane around a moving observer.
limitations: The analysis assumes a depth threshold of 10% is a useful limit for considering contributions to layout perception.
Assumes the observer can look around, register differences on the fovea and retina, and retain information.
Assumes each source pertains to objects of appropriate size that can be easily resolved.
Assumes threshold measurements are informative for everyday, suprathreshold considerations.
The efficacy of depth cues can vary greatly depending on environmental conditions (e.g., air quality for aerial perspective).
Individual differences in information source use are expected, which may affect the utility of virtual reality systems.
Conflicts between information sources (e.g., in pictures) are typically inherent and can compromise generalization from virtual reality to natural perception.
design_implications: Virtual reality (VR) designers must understand natural depth perception to create effective systems.
Different VR system designs should prioritize specific depth cues based on the intended spatial region: personal space (0-1.5m), action space (1.5-30m), or vista space (>30m).

For personal space (e.g., telemedicine), head-mounted displays, geometry engines (for occlusion, size), stereo goggles (for disparities, convergence), and potentially optical adjustments for accommodation are crucial.
For action space (e.g., architectural walk-throughs), larger displays, geometry engines (for occlusion, size, height, motion perspective), and stereo goggles are important.
Designers must be aware that lens length (in photography/cinematography) and field-of-view commands (in computer graphics) significantly alter perceived depth by compressing or dilating space.
VR systems should strive to remove potential information conflicts to mimic everyday perception accurately.
Expect and account for individual differences in how users perceive depth in VR, as people rely on different cues to varying degrees.
